entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: The voiceless *th* /θ/ is made with the tongue tip at the upper teeth while air flows out, with no voice. Said with /s/ instead, *think* becomes *sink* and *thank* becomes *sank*.
entries.usage: Put the tongue tip lightly between the teeth or just behind the upper teeth and blow; the tongue stays flat and relaxed, not grooved as for *s*. German has no /θ/, so German speakers replace it with *s* (sometimes *f*). Practice pairs slowly in front of a mirror: *think/sink, thick/sick, path/pass, mouth/mouse*.
examples: I **think** **three** of us can fit in the back seat.
**Thanks** so much for **thinking** of me on my **birthday**!
A **thick** fog covered the **path**, so we couldn't see a **thing**.

drill.sentence: Our **math** teacher made us **think** about **both** sides of every problem.
drill.hint: Tongue tip at the upper teeth for each *th*; let the air flow, no *s*.

mistake.why: German has no /θ/, so German speakers use the nearest German sound, /s/, and the listener hears a different word.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: The voiced *th* /ð/ in *this, they, other* has the same tongue position as the *th* in *think*, but the voice is on, so you feel a buzz. It starts the most frequent words in English: *the, this, that, they, there*.
entries.usage: Put the tongue tip against the upper teeth and hum through the gap; the air must not stop as it does for *d*. German speakers often say *z* (*zis, zey*) or *d* (*dis, dey*), and both sound strongly accented. Between vowels (*other, mother, weather*) keep it soft and continuous.
examples: **They** told us **the** party is at **their** place **this** year.
My **mother** and **father** moved **there** after they retired.
Can you pass me **that**? No, **the other** one, by the bread.

drill.sentence: **Those** clouds mean **the weather** will change, so bring **that** jacket.
drill.hint: Buzz with the tongue at the teeth in every *th*; no *d* or *z*.

mistake.wrong: Zis is ze one. (/zɪs ɪz zə wʌn/)
mistake.right: This is the one. (/ðɪs ɪz ðə wʌn/)
mistake.why: German has no /ð/, so German speakers use *z* or *d*, the nearest German sounds with voice.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: English *v* /v/ is made with the upper teeth on the lower lip, like German *w* in *Wasser*; English *w* /w/ uses rounded lips and no teeth, like a quick *oo*. Mixing them changes words: *vest/west, vine/wine, vet/wet*.
entries.usage: For *w*, round the lips as for *oo* and open them into the vowel; the teeth must not touch the lip. German speakers often use the German *w* (= English *v*) for English *w*, and some then overcorrect and say *wery* for *very*. Practice pairs: *vine/wine, vet/wet, verse/worse*.
examples: We drove **west** for three hours and stopped in a small **village**.
The **waiter** recommended a **very** good **wine** from a local **vineyard**.
It's **warm** enough this **week** to go out without a **vest**.

drill.sentence: We **visited** a **winery** in **Virginia** last **weekend**.
drill.hint: Teeth on the lip for *v*; rounded lips and no teeth for *w*.

mistake.why: German *w* is the English *v* sound, so German speakers say *v* for *w*, and some then overcorrect *v* into *w*.

entries.term: w after a consonant: quick, twelve, sweet
entries.label: consonant cluster
entries.meaning: In *qu* (/kw/), *tw* and *sw*, the second sound is the rounded-lip /w/ of *we*, not a *v*. German *qu, zw, schw* use a *v*, so *quick* easily becomes *kvick*.
entries.usage: Round your lips already during the *k*, *t* or *s*, so they are in the *w* position when the consonant is released; the lower lip must not touch the teeth. German *Qualität, zwanzig, Schweiz* all have a *v*, which is why *quality, twenty, Switzerland* come out as *kvality, tventy, Svitzerland*. Practice slowly: *k-oo-ick*, then *quick*.
examples: Can I ask a **quick** **question** before we start?
This iced tea is way too **sweet** for me.
My **twin** brother moved to **Sweden** when he was **twenty-two**.

drill.sentence: It was **twelve** degrees outside, so we **quickly** put on our **sweaters**.
drill.hint: Rounded lips, no teeth, in *tw*, *qu* and *sw*.

mistake.why: German *qu, zw, schw* have a *v* sound (*Qual, zwei, schwer*), and learners carry it over.

entries.term: final voiced consonants: bad / bat (German final devoicing)
entries.label: final voicing
entries.meaning: In English, *b, d, g* at the end of a word stay voiced, and the vowel before them is clearly longer. German turns final *b, d, g* into *p, t, k* (*Rad* sounds like *Rat*); English does not.
entries.usage: Keep the voice on through the final consonant and make the vowel before it longer: *bad* sounds almost like *baaad*. If you devoice, *bad* becomes *bat*, *bag* becomes *back*, *cab* becomes *cap*. Vowel length is the main clue American listeners use, so practice pairs and exaggerate it at first.
examples: My **dog** grabbed the **bag** of food off the **bed**.
That **bad** storm knocked a **big** branch onto our **shed**.
Can you **grab** a **cab** and meet us downtown?

drill.sentence: The **kid** **hid** his gym **bag** under the **bed** again.
drill.hint: Long vowel and a voiced *d* or *g* at the end; do not end in *t* or *k*.

mistake.why: German final devoicing (*Rad* sounds like *Rat*) makes learners end these words with *t* and *k*.

entries.label: final voicing
entries.meaning: A final /z/ is a voiced, buzzing *s*, and the vowel before it is longer. It changes meaning: *rise/rice, eyes/ice, lose/loose, prize/price, raise/race*.
entries.usage: Keep the buzz to the very end and lengthen the vowel; a short vowel plus a hissing *s* signals *rice*, not *rise*. In German a final *s* is always voiceless (*Haus, las*), so *lose* comes out as *loose* and *prize* as *price*. The spelling *-se* often hides a /z/: *rise, choose, cause, please*.
examples: Food prices **rise** every year, but my salary doesn't.
Please don't **lose** the keys; we don't have a spare.
Close your **eyes**, and I'll show you the **surprise**.

drill.sentence: The **news** that she won first **prize** came as a big **surprise**.
drill.hint: Long vowel and a buzzing *z* at the end; not *price*.

mistake.why: German has no voiced *s* at the end of a word, so learners devoice it and say a different word.

entries.term: initial s: sun, said, sorry (not z)
entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: At the start of an English word, *s* before a vowel is always a voiceless hiss /s/: *sun, said, sorry, see, so*. A buzzing *z* there turns *sue* into *zoo* and *sip* into *zip*.
entries.usage: In standard German, especially in the north, *s* before a vowel is a voiced *z* (*Sonne, sagen*), and the habit carries over: *zun, zorry, zee you*. Make a sharp hiss with no voice; a hand on your throat should feel no buzz. In English, a word spelled with *s* plus a vowel never starts with /z/.
examples: **Sorry**, I didn't **see** your message until this morning.
The **sun** was **setting** when we finally reached the beach.
She **said** she'd **send** the photos on **Sunday**.

drill.sentence: **Sam** **said** he was **sorry** and **sent** flowers the next day.
drill.hint: A sharp, voiceless hiss at the start of each word; no buzz.

mistake.why: In standard German, *s* before a vowel is voiced (*Sonne*), so learners start these words with a *z*.

entries.term: z vs. ts: zoo, zero, zone
entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: English *z* is a voiced, buzzing /z/, the sound at the end of *buzz*, not the /ts/ that German uses for the letter *z* (*Zoo, Zone*).
entries.usage: Start the buzz with no *t* in front: think of *s* plus voice, like a bee (*zzz-oo*). The trap is words German also has with a *ts* sound: *zoo, zone, zero, zebra, zigzag*. The few exceptions with /ts/ are loanwords such as *pizza* and *mozzarella*.
examples: We took the kids to the **zoo** to see the new **zebras**.
The temperature dropped below **zero** last night.
You're parked in a no-parking **zone**, so you might get a ticket.

drill.sentence: The kids **zigzagged** across the park toward the **zoo** entrance.
drill.hint: A pure buzzing *z*; no *t* before it.

mistake.why: German reads the letter *z* as /ts/ (*Zoo, Zone*), and the familiar loanwords make the habit stronger.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ɪ/ in *ship, live, sit, fill* is short and relaxed, with the tongue a little lower; /i/ in *sheep, leave, seat, feel* is tense and high, with the lips spread as in a smile.
entries.usage: German has a similar pair (*Mitte* vs. *Miete*), but do not rely on length alone: before *p, t, k* the /i/ of *seat* is quite short, so the vowel quality must carry the difference. Mixing them changes meaning: *live/leave, fill/feel, sit/seat, hit/heat*. Watch the spelling too: *been* and *women* have /ɪ/, *machine* and *police* have /i/.
examples: Do you want to **live** downtown, or would you rather **leave** the city?
From the deck of the **ship**, we watched **sheep** on the green hills.
Please fill out this form and take a **seat**; the doctor will **see** you soon.

drill.sentence: If you **sit** in this **seat**, you'll **feel** the **heat** from the fire.
drill.hint: Short, relaxed *i* in *sit*; long, smiling *ee* in *seat*, *feel*, *heat*.

mistake.wrong: I want to leave in Boston. (/liv/ for *live*)
mistake.right: I want to live in Boston. (/lɪv/)
mistake.why: Learners use the tense *ee* or rely on length, but the vowel quality is what separates *live* and *leave*.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /æ/ in *bad, man, had, cat* is made with the jaw wide open and the tongue low and forward; /ɛ/ in *bed, men, head* is the German short *e* of *Bett*. German has no /æ/, so it is the vowel German speakers most often miss.
entries.usage: Start from /ɛ/ and drop the jaw further while keeping the tongue forward; the sound lies between German *ä* and *a*. Without it, *man/men, bad/bed, had/head, sat/set, pan/pen* sound the same. Before *m* and *n* (*man, plan, can*), most Americans make /æ/ longer and a little higher, with a slight glide.
examples: The **man** in the **black** **hat** is my **dad**.
I **had** a **bad** **headache**, so I went to **bed** early.
Can you **lend** me a **pen**? Mine is in my **backpack**.

drill.sentence: My **dad** **sat** **next** to the **band** and **sang** along all night.
drill.hint: Open the jaw wide for *dad, sat, band, sang*; *next* has the smaller *e*.

mistake.why: German has no /æ/, so learners use the German short *e*, and the two words sound the same.

entries.spoken_term: a cup of coffee, a cop car
entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ʌ/ in *cup, luck, hut, but* is a short, relaxed *uh* made in the middle of the mouth; /ɑ/ in *cop, lock, hot, not* is the open *ah* of *father*, with the jaw dropped and the lips unrounded.
entries.usage: For /ʌ/, keep the jaw only half open and the sound short and neutral; for /ɑ/, open wide, as when a doctor asks you to say *ah*. The German *a* lies between the two American vowels, so a full German *a* in *luck* is easily heard as *lock*. Practice *cup/cop, luck/lock, duck/dock, nut/not*.
examples: My **son** wants to be a **cop** when he grows **up**.
Good **luck**, and don't forget to **lock** the door.
It's way too **hot** in that little **hut**; let's sit outside.

drill.sentence: **Mom** **knocked** over a **jug** of juice, and it went all over the **rug**.
drill.hint: Short *uh* in *jug*, *rug*; open *ah* in *Mom*, *knocked*.

mistake.wrong: Good lock! (/lɑk/ for *luck*, said with a full German *a*)
mistake.why: A long, open German *a* sounds like the American /ɑ/, so *luck* is heard as *lock*.

entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: The American /r/ is made with the tongue tip curled up and back, or with the body of the tongue bunched up, so that the tongue touches nothing; the lips are slightly rounded. It is pronounced in every position, also after vowels: *car, here, work*.
entries.usage: Do not roll it or make it in the throat like German *r*, and do not drop it after a vowel as German does (*Bier* sounds like *bee-uh*): Americans say every written *r*. Start from *uh*, then slowly curl the tongue tip back until the sound darkens into *er*. Practice *red, very, car, sorry, world*.
examples: **Rachel**'s **car** is **parked** **right** in front of the **store**.
I'm **really** **sorry**; I completely **forgot** our **dinner** plans.
**Where** are you **from** **originally**, and **where** do you live now?

drill.sentence: My **brother** **drove** **four** hours to go camping by the **river**.
drill.hint: Curl the tongue back for every *r*, also at the end of *brother* and *four*.

mistake.wrong: a throaty German *r*, or kah /kɑ/ for *car*
mistake.right: car /kɑr/, with the tongue curled back
mistake.why: German *r* is made in the throat and disappears after vowels, so learners either use that sound or drop the *r*.

entries.term: the /oʊ/ glide: home, go, phone (not hom)
entries.label: vowel sound
entries.meaning: The American vowel in *home, go, phone, know* is a diphthong: it starts at a mid *o* and glides toward *oo*, with the lips rounding more at the end.
entries.usage: German long *o* in *Sohn* or *Boot* is a pure, steady vowel, and in English it sounds clearly foreign. Start with a relaxed *o* and close the lips toward *oo* during the vowel: *go-oo*. The glide is strongest in stressed syllables and at the end of a word (*go, know, though*).
examples: I left my **phone** at **home**, so **don't** try to call me.
Drive **slowly**; the **road** is still covered in **snow**.
**Joe** says he doesn't **know** where he left his **coat**.

drill.sentence: **Rosie** **wrote** a **note** and **closed** the door quietly.
drill.hint: Let each *o* glide toward *oo*; no flat German *o*.

mistake.why: German long *o* (*Sohn*) has no glide, and a flat *o* is one of the clearest signs of a German accent.

entries.label: word ending
entries.meaning: The past ending *-ed* has three sounds: /t/ after voiceless sounds (*asked, worked, laughed*), /d/ after voiced sounds and vowels (*played, called, lived*), and an extra syllable /ɪd/ only after *t* or *d* (*wanted, needed*).
entries.usage: Do not add a syllable where there is none: *worked* is one syllable, not *work-ed*. German speakers also tend to devoice the /d/, so *played* sounds like *plate* and *lived* like *lift*; keep it voiced and the vowel before it long. The /ɪd/ syllable is weak and short: *WAN-tid*, *NEE-did*.
examples: I **asked** her twice, but she never **answered**.
We **played** cards and **talked** until midnight.
She **wanted** to call, but she **decided** to wait.

drill.sentence: We **stopped** at a diner, **waited** for a table, and **ordered** pancakes.
drill.hint: *stopped* ends in /t/, *ordered* in /d/; only *waited* adds a syllable.

mistake.why: Learners read *-ed* as a syllable, but it is a syllable only after *t* or *d*.

entries.label: word ending
entries.meaning: The plural, possessive and third-person *-s* is /s/ after voiceless sounds (*cats, works, Mike's*), /z/ after voiced sounds and vowels (*dogs, plays, Tom's*), and the extra syllable /ɪz/ after hissing sounds (*buses, watches, George's*).
entries.usage: The /z/ form is the most common one and the one German speakers miss: final devoicing gives every ending a sharp *s*, so *plays* sounds like *place*. Keep the voice on to the end, especially after vowels: *sees, plays, goes*. The /ɪz/ syllable is weak: *BUS-iz*, not *bus-ES*.
examples: My neighbor has two **dogs** and three **cats**.
She **plays** tennis and **watches** soccer on weekends.
All the **buses** were full, so we took two **cabs**.

drill.sentence: He **goes** running, **does** yoga, and **fixes** **bikes** on weekends.
drill.hint: Buzz in *goes*, *does*; an extra syllable in *fixes*; a hiss only in *bikes*.

mistake.why: German final devoicing turns the /z/ ending into /s/, so *plays* sounds like *place*.

entries.label: vowel sound
entries.meaning: The schwa /ə/ is a short, weak *uh* with a relaxed mouth. Most unstressed vowels in English become schwa, whatever the spelling: the *a* in *about*, the *e* in *problem*, the *o* in *today*.
entries.usage: Say the stressed syllable clearly and let the others shrink: *uh-BOUT, PRAH-blum, tuh-DAY*. German speakers tend to pronounce every vowel as written (*prob-LEM, to-DAY*), which sounds over-careful and hides the stress pattern. Short function words are reduced the same way in normal speech: *a, the, to, of, and*.
examples: I'm **about** to leave; can we talk **tomorrow**?
Can you grab **another** **banana** for the smoothie?
The **problem** with **Alaska** is that the summers are so short.

drill.sentence: My **sister** and I **agreed** to **support** each **other**.
drill.hint: Stress *SIS*, *GREED*, *PORT*, *UTH*; the other vowels shrink to *uh*.

mistake.why: Learners pronounce each vowel as spelled, but English reduces unstressed vowels to schwa.

entries.spoken_term: I'm full; don't be a fool
entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ʊ/ in *full, look, pull, good* is short and relaxed, with lightly rounded lips; /u/ in *fool, Luke, pool, food* is tense and long, with the lips pushed forward.
entries.usage: German has a similar pair (*Mutter* vs. *Mut*), so the sounds are not the problem; the spelling is. *Oo* is /ʊ/ in *book, good, look, foot* but /u/ in *food, cool, school*, and *u* is /ʊ/ in *put, pull, full*. Saying *Luke* for *look* or *pool* for *pull* sounds odd and can change the word.
examples: **Look**, there's **Luke** sitting by the **pool** with a **book**.
I'm so **full**; that **food** was really **good**.
**Could** you **put** the **cushions** back on the couch?

drill.sentence: The **cook** **took** the **soup** off the stove to let it **cool**.
drill.hint: Short, relaxed *oo* in *cook*, *took*; long, tense *oo* in *soup*, *cool*.

mistake.why: The spelling *oo* or *u* does not show which vowel it is, and learners default to the long, tense one.

entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: At the end of a syllable (*feel, all, people*) and before a consonant (*milk, help*), American /l/ is dark: the tongue tip touches the ridge behind the teeth while the back of the tongue rises, which gives a hollow, *oo*-like color.
entries.usage: German *l* is light and bright in every position, so *feel* and *milk* sound German when said with it. Keep the tip contact but raise the back of the tongue as for *oo*; American *l* is somewhat dark even at the start of a word. Practice *feel, cool, people, milk, help, world*.
examples: Can you pick up some **milk** and a **bottle** of olive **oil**?
I still don't **feel** **well**, so I'll stay home from **school**.
**Will** you **help** me carry this **table** upstairs?

drill.sentence: **People** in this **small** town are **always** willing to **help**.
drill.hint: Raise the back of the tongue for each *l* at the end of a syllable.

mistake.why: German uses a light *l* everywhere, which sounds foreign at the end of English syllables.

entries.label: final voicing
entries.meaning: *Of* ends in a voiced /v/ and has a short *uh* (/ʌv/, in normal speech /əv/); *off* ends in a voiceless /f/ and has the vowel of *law* (/ɔf/), which many Americans say as the *ah* of *father*.
entries.usage: *Of* is almost always unstressed and short: *a cup of tea* sounds like *a CUP uv TEA*. German final devoicing turns *of* into *off*, and because *of* is so frequent, this is a very noticeable feature of a German accent. Only *off* has a full vowel and an *f*: *turn off, take off, a day off*.
examples: Can I have a cup **of** coffee and a piece **of** cake?
The plane took **off** an hour late because of the fog.
I'm taking the rest **of** the week **off**.

drill.sentence: Most **of** my friends took the day **off** to watch the game.
drill.hint: A short, voiced *uv* in *of*; *awf* (or *ahf*) with an *f* in *off*.

mistake.why: Final devoicing makes German speakers end *of* with an *f*, so it sounds like *off*.

entries.spoken_term: an old jeep, a cheap hotel
entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: /dʒ/ in *jeep, job, German, gym* is a voiced sound, like *d* plus the *zh* of *measure*; /tʃ/ in *cheap, chop, church* is its voiceless partner, the German *tsch*.
entries.usage: Put a hand on your throat: /dʒ/ buzzes from the start, /tʃ/ does not. German has /dʒ/ only in loanwords (*Job, Dschungel*) and often devoices it, so *jeep, job, German* come out as *cheap, chop, Cherman*. In English, *j* is almost always /dʒ/, and so is *g* in many words before *e, i, y* (*gym, age*).
examples: My brother got a **job** at a **gym** in **Jersey** City.
That **jacket** was **cheap**, but it fell apart in a week.
My **German** teacher **changed** schools last **June**.

drill.sentence: **Jake** **chose** the **cheapest** flight and **joined** us at the **beach**.
drill.hint: A voiced, buzzing *j* in *Jake, joined*; a voiceless *ch* in *chose, cheapest, beach*.

mistake.why: German speakers devoice the unfamiliar /dʒ/ and say *tsch* instead.

entries.label: vowel sound
entries.meaning: /ɝ/ is one r-colored vowel, the *er* of *her*, written in many ways: *ir* (*bird, first*), *or* (*word, work*), *ear* (*learn, early*), *ur* (*turn*), *er* (*her*).
entries.usage: There is no separate vowel plus *r*: the tongue is in the *r* position for the whole vowel, tip curled back or body bunched, lips slightly rounded. German speakers often use *ö* (*böd* for *bird*) and drop the *r*; aim for one long, dark *rrr*. Spellings with *o* and *ea* are the trap: *word, world, work* and *learn, earth, heard* all have /ɝ/.
examples: My dad always says the **early** **bird** gets the **worm**.
My daughter's **first** **word** was "dog," not "mom."
It's **worth** **learning** a few **words** before you travel.

drill.sentence: Our **nurse** **turned** **thirty** on **Thursday**, and we got her a cake.
drill.hint: One long, r-colored vowel in each bold word; no German *ö*.

mistake.why: German speakers replace the r-colored vowel with *ö*, drop the *r*, and devoice the final *d*.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: *Work* has the r-colored vowel of *her*; *walk* has the *aw* vowel of *law* and a silent *l*. The spelling misleads: the word with *or* has no *o* sound, and the word with *al* has no *l*.
entries.usage: *Work* is *wurk*, with the tongue curled back for the whole vowel; *walk* is *wawk*, with the jaw open and no *r* or *l*. Many Americans say *walk* with the *ah* of *father* (*wahk*), which is also standard. Mixing them up changes the message: *I'll work from home* and *I'll walk from home* are very different plans.
examples: I usually **walk** to **work** when the weather is nice.
After **work**, I take the dog for a long **walk** around the block.
At ninety, my grandfather still **walks** to the hardware store by himself.

drill.sentence: If the subway isn't **working** tomorrow, I'll just **walk** to the office.
drill.hint: *wurk* with a curled *r*; *wawk* with an open mouth and no *l*.

mistake.why: Learners follow the spelling: they look for an *o* in *work* and an *l* in *walk*.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: *Singer* has only the nasal /ŋ/; *finger* has /ŋ/ plus a real /ɡ/. Words made from an *-ng* verb (*sing, singer; hang, hanger*) have no /ɡ/; most other words with *ng* in the middle (*finger, hungry, English, angry*) have it.
entries.usage: German *Finger* and *Hunger* have no /ɡ/, so German speakers drop it in English and *finger* rhymes with *singer*. After the /ŋ/, release the back of the tongue with a small *g*: *FING-ger, HUNG-gree, ING-glish*. Never add a *g* at the very end of a word: *sing, long, thing*.
examples: The **singer** pointed her **finger** at the crowd and smiled.
I'm so **hungry** that I'm getting **angry**.
My **English** teacher was also a talented **singer**.

drill.sentence: He hurt his **finger** **hanging** pictures and was **angry** all afternoon.
drill.hint: Add a *g* in *finger* and *angry*; none in *hanging*.

mistake.why: German *Finger* has no /ɡ/, and learners carry that over into English.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: *Won't* (= *will not*) has the gliding *oh* of *don't*; *want* has a short, open vowel, which Americans say as /ɑ/, /ɔ/ or /ʌ/ (*wahnt, wawnt, wunt*).
entries.usage: Mixing them up flips the meaning: *I won't go* is the opposite of *I want to go*. *Won't* rhymes with *don't* and needs the full *oh* glide; with a short, flat *o* (*wont*), it can sound like *want*. In casual speech *want to* often becomes *wanna*, which keeps the two further apart.
examples: I **won't** be home for dinner, so don't wait for me.
Do you **want** to split a pizza tonight?
The kids **want** a dog, but my husband says he **won't** walk it.

drill.sentence: I **want** to come, but I **won't** be free until after eight.
drill.hint: *won't* rhymes with *don't*; *want* has a short, open vowel.

mistake.why: A short *o* without the glide is close to the vowel of *want*, so *I won't* may be heard as *I want*.

entries.spoken_term: the letters A, E, and I
entries.label: letter names
entries.meaning: In English the letter A is said /eɪ/ (*ay*), E is /i/ (*ee*) and I is /aɪ/ (*eye*). They sound like German *E*, *I* and *ei*, which makes them easy to mix up when spelling aloud.
entries.usage: This matters when you spell names, email addresses or booking codes on the phone: German speakers often say the German *E* (which sounds like English A) when they mean E, and the German *I* (English E) when they mean I. Practice spelling your own name and address aloud, slowly. On the phone, Americans often add a word to be safe: *A as in apple*.
examples: Is your name spelled with an **I** or an **E**?
Carrots are rich in vitamin **A**, and almonds in vitamin **E**.
My son got an **A** on his science test and was thrilled.

drill.sentence: My last name is Weiss, spelled W, **E**, **I**, double S.
drill.hint: E is *ee*, I is *eye*; do not use the German names.

mistake.wrong: W, *ay*, *ee*, double S (German letter names for *Weiss*)
mistake.why: German *E* sounds like English A and German *I* like English E, so the listener writes down the wrong letters.

entries.label: letter names
entries.meaning: In English, G is said /dʒi/ (*jee*) and J is /dʒeɪ/ (*jay*). Both start with the same /dʒ/; only the vowel is different.
entries.usage: German speakers often mix them up: the German name of G (*geh*) has a vowel close to English *ay*, so G easily comes out as *jay*, and J then gets *jee*. Remember that G rhymes with *B, C, D*, and J rhymes with *A* and *K*. The swap causes real problems with email addresses, passwords and booking codes.
examples: Is that **G** as in golf, or **J** as in Jack?
Turn off the **GPS**; I know a faster way.
His initials are **J. G.**, just like his grandfather's.

drill.sentence: My license plate starts with **G**, **J**, and then the number seven.
drill.hint: G = *jee*, J = *jay*.

mistake.why: The German name of G (*geh*) sounds close to English *jay*, so learners say *jay* for G and then swap J.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: Words such as *breathe, smooth, bathe, soothe* end in the voiced *th* /ð/: tongue at the teeth, voice on. Said with a *z*, *breathe* turns into *breeze*.
entries.usage: Keep the tongue tip at the upper teeth to the very end and keep the voice going; German speakers face a double trap here, because they replace /ð/ with *z* and then devoice it to *s*. The noun *breath* /brɛθ/ has a voiceless *th* and a short *e*; the verb *breathe* /brið/ has a voiced *th* and *ee*. *With* is said with either *th* in American English.
examples: **Breathe** in slowly through your nose, then let it out.
The flight was **smooth** until we got close to Denver.
We **bathe** the baby every night **with** warm water.

drill.sentence: Take a deep **breath**, hold it, and then **breathe** out slowly.
drill.hint: *breath* ends in a voiceless *th*; *breathe* in a voiced *th*, never *z*.

mistake.why: German speakers replace /ð/ with *z*, and final devoicing can then turn it into *s*.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: In *three, thank, thought*, /θ/ is a soft, continuous stream of air between tongue and teeth; /t/ is a short stop and release. Said with a *t*, *three* becomes *tree* and *thank* becomes *tank*.
entries.usage: Do not stop the air: hold the tongue lightly at the teeth and let the air flow before the *r* or vowel. The cluster *thr* (*three, through, throw*) is the hardest; say the *th* first, slowly, then add the curled American *r*. Learners replace /θ/ with *t*, *s* or *f* (*tree, sree, free*), and all three change the word.
examples: We've lived here for **three** years and planted a **tree** each spring.
I just wanted to say **thank** you for the ride.
My **throat** hurts, so I'm skipping practice tonight.

drill.sentence: The kids **threw** **three** snowballs at the old **tree**.
drill.hint: Air through the teeth for *threw*, *three*; a stopped *t* in *tree*.

mistake.why: Without /θ/ in their own language, learners use *t*, *s* or *f*, and *three* becomes another word.

entries.label: consonant cluster
entries.meaning: In words like *months, fifth, sixth, width, depth*, /θ/ sits next to other consonants. It is short here, but dropping it changes the word: *sixth* becomes *six*, *tenths* becomes *tens*.
entries.usage: Move the tongue quickly from the *n, f, d* or *p* to the teeth and let a little air out: *mun-th-s, fif-th*. In fast speech Americans often simplify *months* to something like *munts*, but keep the *th* in ordinal numbers (*fifth, sixth, twelfth*), where it carries the meaning.
examples: We've been waiting for **months** for the new kitchen.
My son is in **fifth** grade this year.
Measure the **width** and **depth** of the closet before you buy shelves.

drill.sentence: Her birthday is on the **sixth**, and his is on the **twelfth** of next **month**.
drill.hint: Keep a short *th* after the consonants: *siks-th, twelf-th, mun-th*.

mistake.why: Learners replace the difficult *th* with *s* or drop it, which merges *sixth* with *six*.

entries.label: final voicing
entries.meaning: A final /v/ is voiced: *save, prove, leave, have, five*. Devoiced to /f/, it becomes another word: *save* turns into *safe*, *prove* into *proof*, *leave* into *leaf*.
entries.usage: Keep the lip-teeth contact and the voice going to the end, and make the vowel before /v/ longer than before /f/. German final devoicing (*brav* is said *braf*) makes this a classic German error, especially in *have, of, five, love*. Noun–verb pairs show the contrast: *belief/believe, proof/prove, grief/grieve, half/halve*.
examples: We're trying to **save** enough to buy a house.
**Steve** **gave** his old **stove** to a neighbor.
The roads are icy, so it's not **safe** to drive.

drill.sentence: We'll **leave** at **five**, so we can **have** dinner before the show.
drill.hint: Keep each final *v* voiced, with a longer vowel before it; no *f*.

mistake.why: German final devoicing turns the final *v* into *f*.

entries.label: final voicing
entries.meaning: A final /dʒ/ in *badge, ridge, age, large, bridge* stays voiced; a final /tʃ/ in *batch, rich, each, watch* is voiceless. The vowel before /dʒ/ is longer.
entries.usage: German has no final /dʒ/ and devoices final consonants, so *badge, age, large, college* come out with a sharp *tsch*. Keep the buzz to the end and lengthen the vowel: *baaadge*. Watch the many words in *-ge* and *-dge*: *edge, judge, change, page, village, knowledge*.
examples: Show your **badge** at the front desk to get in.
We baked a **batch** of cookies for the new neighbors.
What's the **age** limit for the **large** water slide?

drill.sentence: We drove over the **bridge** to a **village** at the **edge** of the lake.
drill.hint: Buzz at the end of *bridge*, *village*, *edge*; no *tch*.

mistake.why: Final devoicing turns the voiced /dʒ/ into /tʃ/, so *age* sounds like the letter H.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /eɪ/ in *late, wait, sale, main* starts at a mid *e* and glides up toward *ee*; /ɛ/ in *let, wet, sell, men* is short and steady, like the German *e* in *Bett*.
entries.usage: German long *e* (*See, Weg*) has no glide, so *late* and *sale* said with it sound German; let the tongue rise toward *ee* during the vowel. With a short, flat *e*, *late* is heard as *let*, *wait* as *wet*, *taste* as *test*. Practice pairs: *late/let, wait/wet, sale/sell, main/men*.
examples: Sorry I'm **late**; **let** me explain what happened.
**Wait** here while I grab an umbrella, or you'll get **wet**.
The store is having a **sale**, but they don't **sell** my size.

drill.sentence: **Let's** **wait** for the **rain** to stop before we **paint** the **fence**.
drill.hint: Glide toward *ee* in *wait, rain, paint*; a short *e* in *let's, fence*.

mistake.wrong: a flat German *e* [leːt] in *late*, or let /lɛt/
mistake.why: German long *e* does not glide, and when it is also short, *late* sounds like *let*.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ʌ/ in *luck, but, much, run* is the short, central *uh*; /ʊ/ in *look, put, book, could* is a short *oo* with lightly rounded lips. The letter *u* can stand for either: *but* vs. *put*.
entries.usage: German speakers sometimes read the letter *u* as a German *u*, so *luck, much, but, up* come out with /ʊ/, and *luck* sounds like *look*. For /ʌ/, keep the lips unrounded and relaxed and the jaw a little open; for /ʊ/, round the lips slightly. Useful pairs: *luck/look, buck/book, tuck/took*.
examples: I **looked** everywhere for my keys, but no **luck**.
I **love** my job, **but** I don't get **much** free time.
**Put** your **book** on the table and **come** eat.

drill.sentence: **Could** you **look** in the **truck** for my **gloves**?
drill.hint: Rounded, short *oo* in *could, look*; open *uh* in *truck, gloves*.

mistake.why: Read with a German *u*, *luck, but, much* get the rounded /ʊ/ instead of the unrounded /ʌ/.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /æ/ in *bag, cat, ran, hat* is a wide-open front vowel; /ʌ/ in *bug, cut, run, hut* is a short, relaxed central *uh*. German has neither vowel.
entries.usage: German speakers tend to use the German *a* for both, so *bag/bug, cat/cut, ran/run, hat/hut* sound alike. For /æ/, spread the lips and push the tongue forward and down; for /ʌ/, relax everything and say a short, lazy *uh*. Practice in short phrases: *I ran, I run; a cap, a cup*.
examples: Help, there's a big **bug** crawling in my **bag**!
The **cat** **ran** under the porch when it heard thunder.
I **cut** my **hand** while opening a **can** of beans.

drill.sentence: **Dad** **ran** to catch the **bus**, **but** it was already gone.
drill.hint: Wide-open *æ* in *Dad, ran*; short *uh* in *bus, but*.

mistake.why: Learners use the German *a* for both vowels and devoice the *g*, so the two words merge.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ɔ/ in *bought, law, caught, saw* is an open *aw* with no glide; /oʊ/ in *boat, low, coat, so* is the rounded *oh* that glides toward *oo*.
entries.usage: Many Americans, especially in the West and among younger speakers, say /ɔ/ like the *ah* of *father* (*caught* sounds like *cot*); both versions are standard, but neither should sound like *oh*. German speakers tend to use a German *o* for both, so *bought* sounds like *boat*, *law* like *low*, *caught* like *coat*. Open the jaw more for /ɔ/ and keep it still; for /oʊ/, round the lips and glide.
examples: We **bought** a small **boat** last summer.
He **caught** a cold because he forgot his **coat**.
I **saw** a great **show** at the theater last night.

drill.sentence: She **thought** the **old** **road** was too **long** to **walk**.
drill.hint: Open, steady *aw* in *thought, long, walk*; a gliding *oh* in *old, road*.

mistake.why: German speakers use a German *o* for /ɔ/, and Americans hear it as the *oh* of *boat*.

entries.term: short o in American English: hot, job, model
entries.label: vowel sound
entries.meaning: In American English, the short *o* in *hot, job, model, stop, got* is /ɑ/, the open, unrounded *ah* of *father*. British English and German use a rounded *o* in these words.
entries.usage: Drop the jaw and keep the lips relaxed, not rounded: *haht, jahb, MAH-dul*. A rounded *o* in *hot* or *not*, as in German *Gott*, is one of the clearest British or German markers in an American accent. The vowel is the same as in *father* and *spa*.
examples: It's so **hot** today that I **stopped** **jogging** after a mile.
He **got** a **job** at a coffee **shop** downtown.
My brother builds **model** airplanes in his free time.

drill.sentence: Can you grab a **box** of **popcorn** on your way home? I **forgot** to get it.
drill.hint: An open, unrounded *ah* in every bold word (in *popcorn*, only the first syllable).

mistake.why: German *o* in *Gott* and the British *o* are rounded; the American vowel is the unrounded *ah* of *father*.

entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: /ʒ/ is the voiced partner of *sh*: the sound of *g* in German *Garage* or *j* in *Journal*, and of the middle of *measure, usual, vision, pleasure, casual*. English usually spells it with *s*.
entries.usage: Make *sh* and add voice: the tongue stays in place and the buzz starts. German speakers often devoice it (*MESH-er, YOO-shoo-ul*) or replace it with the *j* of *jeep*. Common spellings: *-sure* (*measure, pleasure, leisure*), *-sual* (*usual, casual*), *-sion* after a vowel (*vision, decision*).
examples: As **usual**, he was the last one to arrive.
It was a real **pleasure** to meet your parents.
Can you **measure** the window before we buy curtains?

drill.sentence: The kids spent a **leisurely** afternoon digging for **treasure** in the backyard.
drill.hint: A voiced *zh* in *leisurely* and *treasure*; not *sh*.

mistake.why: German has /ʒ/ only in a few loanwords, and speakers often devoice it to *sh*.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: /ʃ/ in *share, wash, shoes* is a smooth, continuous hiss, like German *sch*; /tʃ/ in *chair, watch, choose* starts with a short *t* stop, like German *tsch*.
entries.usage: German has both sounds (*Schule, tschüss*), but it rarely starts a word with *tsch*, so learners easily soften an English *ch* at the start of a word into *sh* (many Germans even say *Chips* with *sch*). Start /tʃ/ with the tongue tip pressed up as for *t*, then release it into *sh*. The spelling *tch* (*watch, kitchen*) is always /tʃ/.
examples: Grab a **chair** and **watch** the game with us.
Do you want to **share** some **chips** and salsa?
I spilled coffee on my **shirt**, so I need to **wash** it.

drill.sentence: **Which** **shoes** should I **choose** for the **beach**?
drill.hint: *ch* starts with a short *t* in *which, choose, beach*; *shoes* is smooth.

mistake.why: German rarely starts a word with *tsch*, so learners soften the /tʃ/ into *sh*.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: /n/ is made with the tongue tip on the ridge behind the upper teeth; /ŋ/ in *thing, sing, long* is made with the back of the tongue against the soft palate, as in German *Ding*. Mixing them changes words: *thin/thing, ran/rang, win/wing*.
entries.usage: German has the same /ŋ/ (*lang, singen*), so the sound itself is easy; keep the tongue tip down so *thing* does not slide into *thin*, and do not add a *k* (*thingk*). End /ŋ/ by simply stopping the voice while the back of the tongue stays up. Practice *thin/thing, win/wing, kin/king*.
examples: He's so **thin** that all his clothes look too big.
The only **thing** I need right now is a good night's sleep.
The phone **rang** just as I **ran** out the door.

drill.sentence: **Bring** a **thin** jacket; the **evening** air can get cool.
drill.hint: The back of the tongue for *bring, evening*; the tongue tip for *thin*.

mistake.why: Learners use the tongue tip or add a *k*, but /ŋ/ is one sound made with the back of the tongue.

entries.term: h at the start: heart / art
entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: English /h/ is a light breath before the vowel, like German *h* in *Haus*. Dropping it changes words: *heart* becomes *art*, *hold* becomes *old*, *hate* becomes *eight*.
entries.usage: German has the same sound, so for German speakers the useful part is where Americans do not say it. The *h* is silent in a few words: *hour, honest, honor, heir*, and for most Americans *herb*. In fast speech Americans also drop it in unstressed *he, him, her, his, have* (*tell 'im*), but never in a stressed word like *heart, hold, hand*.
examples: She has a **heart** of gold and a real love of **art**.
**Hold** on tight; this **old** elevator shakes a lot.
I **hate** it when the bus is **eight** minutes late.

drill.sentence: **Harry** **hurt** his **hand** while **helping** us move the **heavy** couch.
drill.hint: A light breath of *h* before each bold word; do not drop it.

mistake.why: German speakers pronounce every written *h*, but *heir* never has one, and most Americans drop it in *herb*.

entries.term: y at the start: year / ear
entries.label: consonant sound
entries.meaning: *Year* starts with the glide /j/, the German *j* in *ja*; *ear* starts directly with the vowel. Other pairs: *yeast/east, years/ears*.
entries.usage: Before an *ee*-like vowel the *y* is hard to hear, because the tongue is already high; push the tongue up a little more and start with a clear German *j*: *y-eer*. Many learners say *ear* for *year*, or the reverse, so *Happy New Year* can sound like *Happy New Ear*. Practice *year/ear, yeast/east, years/ears*.
examples: My left **ear** has been ringing for almost a **year**.
Add the **yeast** to warm water and wait ten minutes.
I haven't seen my cousin in **years**; she looks totally different.

drill.sentence: Every **year** my **ears** hurt on the long flight to **Europe**.
drill.hint: A clear *y* glide at the start of *year* and *Europe*; *ears* starts with the vowel.

mistake.why: Before the high vowel, learners skip the glide, so *year* and *ear* sound the same.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ɪr/ in *here, near, beer, ear* is a high *ih* followed by the American *r*; /ɛr/ in *there, care, bear, hair* starts lower and more open, like the *e* of *bed*.
entries.usage: The spelling is unreliable: *ear* is /ɪr/ in *hear, near, fear* but /ɛr/ in *bear, wear, pear, swear*. German speakers also tend to drop the *r* (*hee-uh, beh-uh*), which blurs the pairs, so keep the American *r*. Practice *beer/bear, here/hair, fear/fair, cheer/chair*.
examples: We saw a black **bear** **near** the campsite.
**Here**'s your **chair**; I'll get you a **beer**.
What are you going to **wear** to the party this **year**?

drill.sentence: It's not **fair** to **cheer** when a player on the other team gets hurt.
drill.hint: Open *air* in *fair*; high *eer* in *cheer*.

mistake.why: The spelling *ea* leads learners to the *eer* of *hear* and *near*.

entries.label: weak ending
entries.meaning: Unstressed *-er, -or, -ar* at the end of a word all sound the same: a short, weak, r-colored /ɚ/. The *o* in *doctor* and the *a* in *dollar* are not pronounced as vowels of their own.
entries.usage: German *Doktor, Dollar, Motor* keep full vowels (*DOK-tor*), and that habit makes English sound stiff. Say only a quick *er* with the tongue curled: *DAHK-ter, DAH-ler, MOH-ter*. The same weak *er* ends *actor, sugar, color, similar*.
examples: The **doctor** said I need more rest and less coffee.
Everything in that little store costs a **dollar**.
My **neighbor**'s **daughter** is an **actor** in New York.

drill.sentence: The **doctor** charged my **mother** two hundred **dollars** for a ten-minute visit.
drill.hint: Every ending is the same weak, r-colored *er*.

mistake.why: German *Doktor* and *Dollar* keep full vowels; English reduces the unstressed ending to /ɚ/.

entries.label: consonant cluster
entries.meaning: Many English words end in three or four consonants: *asked* /skt/, *texts* /ksts/, *desks* /sks/. The last consonant often carries the grammar, such as the past tense or the plural.
entries.usage: Learners drop the last sound, so *asked* becomes *ask* and *texts* becomes *text*, and the grammar is lost. In relaxed speech Americans themselves simplify (*asked* often sounds like *ast*, *texts* like *teks*), but in careful speech say every consonant. Practice slowly at first: *ask-t, teks-ts, desk-s*.
examples: My mom **asked** whether I'd **locked** the front door.
He sends me about fifty **texts** a day, mostly jokes.
The library replaced all the old **desks** over the summer.

drill.sentence: She **asked** about the **tests**, so I sent her two **texts** with the **results**.
drill.hint: Say every final consonant: *askt, tests, teksts*.

mistake.why: Learners drop the last consonant of the cluster, and with it the past tense or the plural.

entries.label: consonant contrast
entries.meaning: /v/ is a continuous, buzzing sound made with the upper teeth on the lower lip; /b/ is a stop: both lips close, then open. *Vote/boat, very/berry, van/ban, curve/curb* are different words.
entries.usage: German has both sounds, so the contrast is easy for German speakers; it is a classic problem for Spanish or Japanese speakers, who often use *b* for both. Two points still matter for Germans: the letter *v* is always /v/, never the /f/ of German *Vater*, and at the end of a word both stay voiced: *curve* is not *curf*, and *curb* is not *curp*.
examples: The board will **vote** on the **budget** next week.
He took the **curve** too fast and hit the **curb**.
These **berries** are **very** sweet this year.

drill.sentence: **Ben** **bought** a **van** so he could **visit** his **brother** **every** weekend.
drill.hint: Teeth on the lip for *van, visit, every*; both lips for *Ben, bought, brother*.

mistake.why: German final devoicing turns a final /v/ into /f/ and a final /b/ into /p/.

entries.spoken_term: the letters R, Y, and Z
entries.label: letter names
entries.meaning: In American English, R is /ɑr/ (*ar*, as in *car*), Y is /waɪ/ (like *why*) and Z is /zi/ (*zee*). British English says *zed* for Z.
entries.usage: German *R* (*err*), *Y* (*Ypsilon*) and *Z* (*tset*) are easy to fall back on when you spell names or codes under pressure. *Zee* is so standard in the US that *zed* sounds clearly British, and a German *tset* will confuse the listener. The American R needs the curled American *r* at the end: *arr*, not *ah*.
examples: That movie is rated **R**, so the kids can't see it.
We saved a lot of money with a **DIY** bathroom remodel.
My nephew is **Gen Z**, so he never answers phone calls.

drill.sentence: Our hotel confirmation code is **R**, **Y**, **Z**, seven, seven.
drill.hint: R = *ar*, Y = *why*, Z = *zee*.

mistake.wrong: *err* for R, *ipsilon* for Y, *tset* or *zed* for Z
mistake.why: Under pressure, learners fall back on the German letter names, or on the British *zed* they learned at school.

entries.label: consonant cluster
entries.meaning: The comparatives and superlatives of *long, strong, young* add a /ɡ/ after the /ŋ/: *longer, strongest, younger*. The base words themselves end in a plain /ŋ/ with no /ɡ/.
entries.usage: This breaks the *singer* rule, so learn it as an exception: *longer* (more long) has /ɡ/, but *longing* and *singer* do not. German *länger* and *jünger* have no /ɡ/, so German speakers drop it. Release the back of the tongue with a soft *g* before the *-er*.
examples: The days are getting **longer** now that it's spring.
She's **younger** than me, but she's much **stronger**.
This is the **strongest** coffee I've ever had.

drill.sentence: My **younger** brother can run **longer** than I can, even uphill.
drill.hint: Add a *g* before *-er*: *YUNG-ger, LAWNG-ger*.

mistake.why: German *länger* and *jünger* have no /ɡ/, and the *singer* rule misleads learners too.

entries.label: vowel sound
entries.meaning: In American English, *ask, after, class, dance, can't, bath, half* have the /æ/ of *cat*. Southern British English uses the long *ah* of *father* in these words.
entries.usage: Many Germans learned British English at school and say *ahsk, AHF-ter, clahss*, which is not wrong but sounds out of place in an otherwise American accent. Use the wide-open /æ/. Before *n* and *m* (*dance, can't, answer*), most Americans make it longer and a bit higher, with a slight glide.
examples: Can I **ask** you something **after** **class**?
My parents still go **dancing** every Friday night.
I **can't** eat more than **half** of this pizza.

drill.sentence: I **can't** make it to **dance** **class** tonight; my **calf** still hurts.
drill.hint: The *æ* of *cat* in every bold word; no British *ah*.

mistake.why: German schools often teach British English, which uses the *ah* of *father* in these words.

entries.label: vowel contrast
entries.meaning: /ɑr/ in *farm, card, heart, star* is the open *ah* plus the American *r*; /ɔr/ in *form, cord, horse, more* is a rounded *o* plus *r*. Pairs: *farm/form, card/cord, barn/born, far/for*.
entries.usage: For /ɑr/, drop the jaw first and then curl the tongue; for /ɔr/, round the lips first. Two spelling traps: *heart* has /ɑr/, and after *w* the letters *ar* are /ɔr/: *war, warm, award, quarter*. German speakers who drop the *r* (*fahm, fohm*) lose half of the difference.
examples: My grandparents had a **farm** with ten **horses**.
Please fill out this **form** and attach a copy of your **card**.
My **heart** was racing when the **storm** hit.

drill.sentence: The **farmer** drove the **horses** into the **barn** before the **storm**.
drill.hint: Open *ar* in *farmer, barn*; rounded *or* in *horses, storm*.

mistake.why: After *w*, the spelling *ar* is said /ɔr/ (*war, warm, quarter*); German *warm* makes the *ah* very tempting.

entries.label: word ending
entries.meaning: A small set of adjectives ending in *-ed* have the extra syllable /ɪd/ even though no *t* or *d* comes before it: *naked, wicked, rugged, crooked, sacred, wretched*. They break the normal *-ed* rule.
entries.usage: Learn them as whole words: *NAY-kid, WIK-id, RUG-id, KROOK-id*. A few change with meaning: *aged* is *AY-jid* in *my aged parents* but one syllable in *aged ten* or *aged cheese*, and *learned* is *LUR-nid* when it means *scholarly*.
examples: The baby ran through the house **naked** after his bath.
The **wicked** stepmother is the best part of the play.
We hiked along a **rugged** stretch of coast in Maine.

drill.sentence: The **crooked** old cabin stood alone on a **rugged** hillside.
drill.hint: Each *-ed* here is a full syllable: *KROOK-id, RUG-id*.

mistake.why: Learners apply the normal *-ed* rule (*baked* /beɪkt/), but these adjectives keep an old extra syllable.
